description_full: Blue Bird Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, designs, engineers, manufactures, and sells school buses in the United States, Canada, and internationally. The company operates through two segments, Bus and Parts. It offers Type C, Type D, and specialty buses; and alternative power options through its propane powered, gasoline powered, compressed natural gas powered, and electric powered school buses, as well as diesel engines. The company also sells replacement bus parts; and provides extended warranties related to its products. Blue Bird Corporation sells its products through drop ship and a network of dealers, as well as directly to fleet operators, the United States government, and state governments; independent service centers; and maintains a parts distribution center. It has a collaboration with Ford Motor Company to create the next generation of F-53/F-59 commercial stripped chassis. Blue Bird Corporation was founded in 1927 and is headquartered in Macon, Georgia.

financial_summary: Blue Bird Corporation is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.9B market cap on $1.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +23% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 29% against a 10% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $153M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.38× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 23× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

At current returns, reinvesting 76% of profits supports about 22.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
